#### Goal:
Developing working knowledge of linear models in R: fitting them, reading diagnostic plots, and judging when a model is (or is not) correctly specified.


#### sample Simulation foundations on a linear and quadratic  terms.
general approach;

- Create the simulated dataset.
- Fit the three linear models described above.
- Use the predict() function to obtain observed and fitted values.
- Use the resid() function to obtain residual values.
- Plot the observed and fitted data points, as well as the residual values.


```{r}
# Starting with default variables to assess association between x and y
# General f(x) = 20 + 10*x + 5x^2 to test with models.
# + noise = rnorm(100, 0, 1.5)
x <- 1:20
y <- 20 + 10 * 1:20 + 5 * (1:20)^2 + rnorm(20, 0, 200)
dfr <- data.frame(x, y)

fx <- 20 + 10 * x + 5 * x^2 # function without noise
fxn <- 20 + 10 * 1:20 + 5 * (1:20)^2 + rnorm(20, 0, 200) # function + noise


# model 1; m1 :  intercept only (y~1) ;

m1 <- lm(y ~ 1, data = dfr)
summary(m1)
# model 2; m2 : intercept and slope (y~x)

m2 <- lm(y ~ x, data = dfr)
summary(m2)
# model 3, m3 = intercept, slope, and curvature,quadratic term x^2 #(y~x+I(x^2)).

m3 <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2), data = dfr)
summary(m3)

#----predicting observed values
m1.obs <- predict(m1)
m2.obs <- predict(m1)
m3.obs <- predict(m1)

#---- obtaining residuals values

m1.resid <- resid(m1)
m2.resid <- resid(m2)
m3.resid <- resid(m3)

# plotting observed and fitted + residuals

for (i in 1:3) {
  lms <- list(m1, m2, m3)[[i]] # model i
  plot(dfr$x, dfr$y,
    pch = 19,
    xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
    main = c("(1) y ~ 1", "(2) y ~ x", "(3) y ~ x + I(x^2)")[i]
  )
  lines(dfr$x, fx, lty = 2, col = "grey50") # default
  points(dfr$x, predict(lms), col = "red", pch = 20) # fitted points
  lines(dfr$x, predict(lms), col = "red") # fitted shape
}


for (i in 1:3) {
  lms <- list(m1, m2, m3)[[i]]
  plot(fitted(lms), resid(lms),
    pch = 19,
    xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
    main = c("(1) y ~ 1", "(2) y ~ x", "(3) y ~ x + I(x^2)")[i]
  )
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
  lines(lowess(fitted(lms), resid(lms)), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
}


compare <- data.frame(
  model = c("(1) y ~ 1", "(2) y ~ x", "(3) y ~ x + I(x^2)"),
  intercept = c(coef(m1)[1], coef(m2)[1], coef(m3)[1]),
  slope.x = c(NA, coef(m2)[2], coef(m3)[2]),
  coef.x2 = c(NA, NA, coef(m3)[3]),
  sigma = c(
    summary(m1)$sigma, summary(m2)$sigma,
    summary(m3)$sigma
  ),
  R.squared = c(
    summary(m1)$r.squared, summary(m2)$r.squared,
    summary(m3)$r.squared
  ),
  adj.R.squared = c(
    summary(m1)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(m2)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(m3)$adj.r.squared
  ),
  RSS = c(sum(m1.resid^2), sum(m2.resid^2), sum(m3.resid^2))
)
```
From the data simulation, model 1 and 2 appears to significantly explain the variability in y (p-value = c( 0.000232 *** , 2.41e-10 *** )  respectively.). However, when model 3( I(x^2)) is introduced, the the earlier observed influenced in m1 and m2 disappears leaving a fairly significant explained variability in the in y.( p-value = 0.00174 **)
From the diagnostic plots, the data set in model 3 (m3 ~  y~x + I(x^2)) appears to be the only normally distributed fit, based on the QQ plot. 
assessing each model individually,the variability accounted for by each model, m1,m2,m3 were 0% , 89% , 94% respectively. Though there's large effect size in the models, the noise might be a contributing factor.



#### Part B: Applying it to real data( GEO dataset ) 

```{r}
# functions

GEODataDownload <- function(DS, gpl, gsm, PlateAnnotInfo, GenerateMetaData, Technology) {
  library(DESeq2)
  library(limma)
  library(data.table)
  if (Technology == "Array") {
    gset <- getGEO(DS)
    if (length(gset) > 1) idx <- grep(gpl, attr(gset, "names")) else idx <- 1
    gset <- gset[[idx]]
    fvarLabels(gset) <- make.names(fvarLabels(gset))
    comp <- gsub(" ", "", gsm)
    comp <- gsub(",", "", comp)
    gsms <- paste0(comp)
    #### Set up raw names ####
    sml <- c()
    for (i in 1:nchar(gsms)) {
      sml[i] <- substr(gsms, i, i)
    }
    ex <- exprs(gset)
    qx <- as.numeric(quantile(ex, c(0., 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99, 1.0), na.rm = T))
    LogC <- (qx[5] > 100) ||
      (qx[6] - qx[1] > 50 && qx[2] > 0) ||
      (qx[2] > 0 && qx[2] < 1 && qx[4] < 2)
    if (LogC) {
      ex[which(ex <= 0)] <- NaN
      exprs(gset) <- log2(ex)
    }
    sml <- paste("G", sml, sep = "")
    f1 <- as.factor(sml)
    gset$description2 <- f1
    design <- model.matrix(~ description2 + 0, gset)
    colnames(design) <- levels(f1)
    fit <- lmFit(gset, design)
    cont.matrix <- makeContrasts(G1 - G0, levels = design)
    fit2 <- contrasts.fit(fit, cont.matrix)
    fit2 <- eBayes(fit2, 0.01)
    tT <- topTable(fit2, adjust = "fdr", sort.by = "B", number = 25000000000)
    #### subset ####
    ex2 <- data.table(subset(tT, select = c("ID", "logFC", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val")))
    ex2$ID <- as.character(ex2$ID)
    #### annotate with gene names ####
    plat <- PlateAnnotInfo[GPLID == gpl, ][, !"GPLID", with = FALSE]
    if (nrow(plat) == 0) {
      print(paste("There is no annotation information available for", gpl))
    }
    plat$ID <- as.character(plat$ID)
    plat <- plat[!duplicated(plat$ID), ]
    ex2 <- merge(plat, ex2, by = "ID")
    ex2$ID <- as.character(ex2$ID)
    exraw <- data.table(ex)
    exraw$ID <- as.character(rownames(ex))
    #### annotate raw data with gene names ####
    ex2 <- merge(ex2, exraw, by = "ID")
    #### Generate Meta Data ####
    Pdat <- pData(gset)
    #### Add Meta data ####
    Pdat <- as.data.table(Pdat)
    return(list(Data = ex2, MetaData = Pdat))
  }

  if (Technology == "RNAseq") {
    ACC <- paste("acc=", DS, sep = "")
    file <- paste("file=", DS, "_raw_exprs_GRCh38.p13_NCBI.tsv.gz", sep = "")
    comp <- gsub(" ", "", gsm)
    comp <- gsub(",", "", comp)
    gsms <- paste0(comp)
    #### Set up DEG names ####
    urld <- "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?format=file&type=rnaseq_exprs"
    path <- paste(urld, ACC, file, sep = "&")
    tbl <- as.matrix(data.table::fread(path, header = T, colClasses = "integer"), rownames = "GeneID")
    exraw <- tbl
    apath <- paste(urld, "type=rnaseq_exprs", "file=Human.GRCh38.p13.annot.tsv.gz", sep = "&")
    annot <- tryCatch(data.table::fread(apath, header = T, quote = "", stringsAsFactors = F, data.table = F),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    ## FALLBACK (only change to the notes' function): if NCBI serves a captcha page instead of the
    ## annotation file, use NCBI's Homo_sapiens.gene_info (the same GeneID/Symbol/description source)
    if (is.null(annot) || !all(c("GeneID", "Symbol", "Description") %in% names(annot))) {
      annot <- data.table::fread("https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/DATA/GENE_INFO/Mammalia/Homo_sapiens.gene_info.gz",
        header = T, quote = "", stringsAsFactors = F, data.table = F
      )
      names(annot)[names(annot) == "#tax_id"] <- "tax_id"
      annot <- annot[, c("GeneID", "Symbol", "description")]
      names(annot)[3] <- "Description"
    }
    rownames(annot) <- annot$GeneID
    sml <- strsplit(gsms, split = "")[[1]]
    sel <- which(sml != "X")
    sml <- sml[sel]
    tbl <- tbl[, sel]
    gs <- factor(sml)
    groups <- make.names(c("Ctrl", "Tx"))
    levels(gs) <- groups
    sample_info <- data.frame(Group = gs, row.names = colnames(tbl))
    keep <- rowSums(tbl >= 10) >= min(table(gs))
    tbl <- tbl[keep, ]
    ds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = tbl, colData = sample_info, design = ~Group)
    ds <- DESeq(ds, test = "Wald", sfType = "poscount")
    r <- results(ds, contrast = c("Group", groups[2], groups[1]), alpha = 0.05, pAdjustMethod = "fdr")
    tT <- r[order(r$padj)[1:length(r$padj)], ]
    tT <- merge(as.data.frame(tT), annot, by = 0, sort = F)
    tT <- subset(tT, select = c("GeneID", "padj", "pvalue", "lfcSE", "stat", "log2FoldChange", "baseMean", "Symbol", "Description"))
    #### subset ####
    ex2 <- data.table(subset(tT, select = c("GeneID", "Symbol", "Description", "log2FoldChange", "pvalue", "padj")))
    #### Adjust column names ####
    setnames(ex2, c("GeneID", "Symbol", "Description"), c("ENTREZID", "SYMBOL", "GENENAME"))
    #### Get Raw data ####
    GeneID <- as.integer(rownames(exraw))
    exraw <- as.data.table(exraw)
    #### Update column names ####
    exraw$ENTREZID <- GeneID
    #### merge FC and raw data together ####
    mer <- merge(ex2, exraw, by = "ENTREZID")
    return(mer)
  }
}
```


#### 2: loading data

```{r}
library(GEOquery)
library(data.table)


##
gse <- getGEO("GSE19420")[[1]]
metadata <- pData(gse)
expr <- exprs(gse)

identical(colnames(expr), metadata$geo_accession) # checking if both matches

## -Clean metadata ----
metadata$group <- sub("group: ", "", metadata$characteristics_ch1)
metadata$age <- as.numeric(sub("age: ", "", metadata$characteristics_ch1.1))
metadata$bmi <- as.numeric(sub("bmi: ", "", metadata$characteristics_ch1.2))

## ---- 3. Loop: one linear model per gene ---------------------------
cont_var <- metadata$bmi # the continuous dependent variable

results <- data.frame(
  probe = rownames(expr),
  slope = NA,
  pvalue = NA
)

for (i in 1:nrow(expr)) {
  fit <- lm(cont_var ~ expr[i, ])
  results$slope[i] <- coef(fit)[2]
  results$pvalue[i] <- anova(fit)[["Pr(>F)"]][1]
}

hist(results$pvalue,
  col = "purple",
  main = "Distribution of ANOVA p-values across all genes (bmi ~ expression)",
  xlab = "p-values(ANOVA)"
)

# assessing e most extreme genes

# summary(results$pvalue)


#      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.       NAs
# 0.0000492 0.2337905 0.4840769 0.4914808 0.7475298 0.9999971      4397

smallest_p_loc <- which.min(results$pvalue) # location of smallest pvalue
biggest_p_loc <- which.max(results$pvalue) # location of largest pvalue

results[smallest_p_loc, ]
results[biggest_p_loc, ]

# Most significant: model summary, ANOVA, diagnostics

fit_most <- lm(cont_var ~ expr[smallest_p_loc, ])
summary(fit_most)
anova(fit_most)

# plot of extreme with the smallest pvalue
genes_table <- Table(getGEO("GPL570"))

most_sig_gene <- genes_table[smallest_p_loc, "Gene Symbol"]
most_sig_gene
least_sig_gene <- genes_table[biggest_p_loc, "Gene Symbol"]
least_sig_gene

plot(expr[smallest_p_loc, ], cont_var,
  pch = 19, col = "green",
  main = paste("bmi vs expression Gene_Name = ", most_sig_gene),
  xlab = "Gene Expression", ylab = "bmi"
)
abline(fit_most, col = "red", lwd = 2)


par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit_most)

#-#Least significant: model summary, ANOVA, diagnostics
fit_least <- lm(cont_var ~ expr[biggest_p_loc, ])
summary(fit_least)
anova(fit_least)

# plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

plot(expr[biggest_p_loc, ], cont_var,
  pch = 19, col = "red",
  main = paste("bmi vs expression Gene_Name = ", least_sig_gene),
  xlab = "Gene Expression", ylab = "bmi"
)
abline(fit_least, col = "green", lwd = 2)

# diagnostic plots

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit_least)
```

**Discussion and conclusion**
Based on the problem, the Null and Alternative hypothesis are set as;
- H0: genes expression level and BMI are independent
- HA: genes expression level and BMI are not independent

Based on the on the linear model fit across genes, the most extreme genes considered to have some effect on the association between Gene expression and BMI were "EIF5" and "TRG-AS1". 
EIF5 based on linear model fit and anova shows a negative ( slope = -8.991 ) and and adjusted effect size of about 32%. ANOVA should a significant association between the 2 variables ( p-value = 4.92e-05), suggesting evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
In "TRG-AS1" , the model find barely to no relationship between bmi and TRG-AS1, returning a slope = 4.136e-06
and an  effect size (R-squared:  -0.025 ). ANOVA returns a p-value = 1, suggesting evidence for the null hypothesis. Hence we conclude that this particular gene (TRG-AS1) has the least effect on the relationship between bmi and gene expression. Diagnostic plots in EIF5 follows the. normal distribution, better variance compared to TRG-AS1.


#### 3 LOESS and GAM for the top gene, compared with the linear fit

```{r}
library(mgcv)


bmi <- cont_var # y-var
most_sig_gene_exp <- as.numeric(expr[smallest_p_loc, ]) # x_var

fit_most <- lm(cont_var ~ most_sig_gene_exp) # gene = EIF5
fit_loess <- loess(cont_var ~ most_sig_gene_exp, span = 0.5)
fit_gam <- gam(bmi ~ s(most_sig_gene_exp), method = "REML")
summary(fit_gam)
```

```{r}
g.seq <- seq(min(most_sig_gene_exp), max(most_sig_gene_exp), length.out = 200)
pred.lm <- predict(fit_most, newdata = data.frame(most_sig_gene_exp = g.seq))
pred.loess <- predict(fit_loess, newdata = data.frame(most_sig_gene_exp = g.seq))
pred.gam <- predict(fit_gam, newdata = data.frame(most_sig_gene_exp = g.seq))

plot(most_sig_gene_exp, bmi,
  pch = 16, col = "purple", cex = 0.8,
  xlab = "EIF5 expression", ylab = "bmi",
  main = "208708_x_at (EIF5): linear vs LOESS vs GAM"
)
lines(g.seq, pred.lm, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(g.seq, pred.loess, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
lines(g.seq, pred.gam, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Linear regression", "LOESS (span=0.5)", "GAM (REML)"),
  col = c("red", "darkorange", "steelblue"), lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 1, 1)
)

# Model comparison: linear vs. GAM using AIC:

lm.aic <- AIC(fit_most)
lm.aic
gam.aic <- AIC(fit_gam)
gam.aic
rss_loess <- sum(resid(fit_loess)^2)
n <- length(most_sig_gene_exp)

loess.aic <- n * log(rss_loess / n) + n * (log(2 * pi) + 1) +
  2 * (fit_loess$trace.hat + 1)
loess.aic
diffs <- lm.aic - c(loess.aic, gam.aic)
diffs
```

**AIC conclusion:** 
Based on the AIC values, the GAM does not reveal any significant improvement compared to the linear model as they both return similar AIC values.
GAM only confirms what the linear model already suggests. The loess model, however shows some deviation from the linear model, but this may be due to noise, 
rather than a signal.

#### 4. gene-by-gene analysis after normalization

```{r}
library(limma)
expr_norm <- normalizeBetweenArrays(expr, method = "quantile")

# normalized vs unnormalized  boxplot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(expr, col = "red", main = "Unnormalized Log2 Expression")
boxplot(expr_norm, col = "lightgreen", main = "Normalized Log2 Expression")
```

```{r}
# Linear model on normalized expression values

norm_pvalues <- data.frame(
  probe = rownames(expr_norm),
  slope = NA,
  pvalue = NA
)

for (i in 1:nrow(expr_norm)) {
  fit <- lm(cont_var ~ expr_norm[i, ])
  norm_pvalues$slope[i] <- coef(fit)[2]
  norm_pvalues$pvalue[i] <- anova(fit)[["Pr(>F)"]][1]
}

hist(norm_pvalues$pvalue,
  col = "purple",
  main = "Distribution of ANOVA p-values across all genes (bmi ~ expression) normalized",
  xlab = "p-values(ANOVA)"
)
smallest_p_loc_norm <- which.min(norm_pvalues$pvalue) # location of smallest pvalue
biggest_p_loc_norm <- which.max(norm_pvalues$pvalue) # location of largest pvalue

norm_pvalues[smallest_p_loc_norm, ]
norm_pvalues[biggest_p_loc_norm, ]

# most significant p-value after normalization and it's gene name
fit_norm_most <- lm(cont_var ~ expr_norm[smallest_p_loc_norm, ])
summary(fit_norm_most)
anova(fit_norm_most) # Adjusted R-squared:  0.3461


# least significant p-value after normalization and it's gene name
fit_norm_least <- lm(cont_var ~ expr_norm[biggest_p_loc_norm, ])
summary(fit_norm_least)
anova(fit_norm_least) #

# gene names for the top and bottom genes
gene_names_norm <- Table(getGEO("GPL570"))

top_gene_norm <- gene_names_norm[smallest_p_loc_norm, "Gene Symbol"]
top_gene_norm
bottom_gene_norm <- gene_names_norm[biggest_p_loc_norm, "Gene Symbol"]
bottom_gene_norm
```

####  Does normalization have any impact on the p-value?

- H0: mean p-value before normalization = mean p-value after normalization
- HA: mean p-value before normalization != mean p-value after normalization


```{r}
# Top 1000 p-values from both normalized and unnormalized data
library(ggplot2)

top_p_values_raw <- head(results$pvalue[!is.na(results$pvalue)], 1000)
top_p_values_norm <- head(norm_pvalues$pvalue[!is.na(norm_pvalues$pvalue)], 1000)

# testing normality
qqplot(top_p_values_raw, top_p_values_norm)
shapiro.test(top_p_values_raw)
shapiro.test(top_p_values_norm)

# Performing paired t-test to compare the p-values since data is normally distributed
t.test(top_p_values_raw, top_p_values_norm, alternative = "two.sided", paired = T) # p-value = 9.511e-08

# scatter plot
library(ggplot2)


dfr_comparison <- data.frame(raw = top_p_values_raw, norm = top_p_values_norm)

# before normalization
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
ggplot(data = dfr_comparison, aes(x = raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of p-values before normalization",
    x = "P-values before normalization",
    y = "Frequency"
  )

# after normalization
ggplot(data = dfr_comparison, aes(x = norm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "green", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of p-values after normalization",
    x = "P-values after normalization",
    y = "Frequency"
  )

# before and after normalization
ggplot(data = dfr_comparison, aes(x = raw, y = norm)) +
  geom_point(color = "gray50", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 1000 p-values before vs after normalization",
    x = "P-values before normalization",
    y = "P-values after normalization"
  )
```

**Conclusion:**

comparing the p-values before and after normalization, a paired t-test shows a statistically significant 
difference between the two, with a p-value of 9.511e-08. This suggests that normalization
 has a significant impact on the p-values.
 Assessing the raw pvalues and normalized pvalues using boxplot, pvalues in the normalized gene expressions 
 are observed to be more uniformly distributed compared to the raw pvalues.
 Also, after normalization the gene with the most significant effect on BMI (EIF5) shows an improved
 Adjuested effecy size (from 32% to about 34.61%). Gene with the worst association ( prev. TRG-AS1) changed to 
 "CPLX3", this shows the previous one improved in p-value. A scatter plot of normalized vs unnormalized pvalues 
 shows a strong + linear relationship between the two.
 Since shifts in gene expression profiles distribution may be technical and have biological relevance, the normalization 
 process results will be more trustworthy, though it is important to always consider other factors when conducting further analyses.

#### 5. Relationship between the fitted and observed values for trust in linear model results

```{r}
# observed vs fitted values for the most significant gene after normalization
obs_trusted <- as.numeric(expr_norm[smallest_p_loc_norm, ])
fit_trusted <- lm(cont_var ~ obs_trusted)
summary(fit_trusted)
anova(fit_trusted)

pred_trusted <- predict(fit_trusted)
res_trusted <- resid(fit_trusted)

# fitted vs observed plot
plot(pred_trusted, cont_var,
  pch = 19, col = "lightblue",
  xlab = "Fitted bmi (from EIF5 expression)",
  ylab = "Observed bmi",
  main = "Fitted vs observed — (EIF5), normalized values"
)
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lty = 2)
legend("topright", "y = fitted (perfect fit)", lty = 2, col = "red")
cor(pred_trusted, cont_var)

# shapiro-wilk test on residuals and diagnostic plots for regression assumptions
# Normality, equal variance and linearity
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pred_trusted, res_trusted,
  main = "Residuals vs Fitted (EIF5)",
  xlab = "Fitted bmi (from EIF5 expression)",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  pch = 19,
  col = "lightblue"
)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

qqnorm(res_trusted)
qqline(res_trusted, col = "green")
shapiro.test(res_trusted) # normalized
shapiro.test(resid(fit_most)) # unnormalized/raw
```

**Results:**
The trustworthy fitted model vs observed show a strong psotive correlation with about 34.6% Adj. R-squared 
and correlation coefficient of 0.6017. This means that the gene EIF5 can explain about 34.6% of the variation in BMI.
along with QQ plot, fitted vs residuals shows plots with fairly normal distribution of residuals.(p-value= 0.05035) and it's same
for the non-normalized data (p-value=0.01553- shapiro.test) with a fair amount of spread.
In terms of taking the normalized model's results are face values, the regression assumptions are barely
supported, so i'd suggest the p-value / data be need a second look or at least be interpreted with caution.
